The letters mem and samekh, nun and…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 10, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sukkah 52b) to illuminate his argument here (“as our Sages of blessed memory stated (Sukkah 52b), this divine help is channeled through the woman whom Scripture identifies as divinely designated for help; and under the condition: "if he merits, she is a helper...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: But in truth, although man's body is below in this world, his soul is rooted on High; and all Israel have a share in the World to Come (Sanhedrin 90a), meaning that the soul is anchored to its root in that world, unless severed through sins. And the inception of defilement begins with a minuscule lapse, drawing iniquity with cords of vanity (Yeshayah 5:18); as stated in Sukkah (52b): "the yetzer hara initially resembles a spider's web, and ultimately becomes like cart-ropes".
column15: When in truth it is divine grace that graciously attributes the initiative to creation. And to this our Sages alluded in Eruvin (65a): “Whoever is appeased through his wine possesses of the mind of his Creator.” “Wine” denotes bold certainty; and when Hashem illuminates certainty in the heart that man is a beloved child of God, yet he rests not in that privilege, yielding instead to conduct himself with the humble constriction of a servant before his master—which stirs deeper mercy.

column13: And similarly He gave him a foretaste of the vast elevation of physical pleasures sanctified for Heaven's sake, which in their highest sublimation partake of the World to Come; and precisely into this state "Sheba fell", for here the dark force finds its foothold. And as is likewise expounded in Chapter Chelek regarding the Generation of the Flood, that He gave them a taste of the World to Come, yet their downfall was through licentiousness, because illicit passion mirrors the intense ecstasy of the World to Come—one being the holy Eshet Chayil and the other the impure Eshet Zenunim; and the Eshet Zenunim mimics the guise of the Eshet Chayil to gain a grip…
column15: For the concept of upper and lower waters is this: the upper waters stand in immense clarity before Hashem, whereas the lower waters represent concealment, where the mind of man becomes intensely perturbed and disoriented. And the source of this turmoil is because, as found in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (ch. 10) and Midrash Tanchuma, Jonah ben Amittai said: “We do not find His overt glory in the sea.”

column11: Taanit 7a: ‘Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said: Why are Torah matters likened to a tree, as it is stated: “It is a tree of life to them who lay hold upon it” (Proverbs 3:18)? This verse comes to tell you that just as a small piece of wood can ignite a large piece, so too, minor Torah scholars can sharpen great Torah scholars and enable them to advance in their studies. And this is what Rabbi Ḥanina said: I have learned much from my teachers and even more from my friends, but from my students I have learned more than from all of them.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 10, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Taanit 7a) to illuminate his argument here (“mirroring: "and from my disciples more than from them all" (Ta'anit 7a), for there was a union of masculine and feminine between him and his disciples; and also within himself, in that the master requires heavenly...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
column13: Whereupon the returning echo born within him from the Shema becomes the voice of Prayer that follows, the quality of the prayer mirroring the depth of his awakening in the Shema; just as the Oral Torah is the returning echo of the Written Torah, so Prayer is the returning echo of the Shema, as in "and from my disciples more than from all" (Ta'anit 7a), where the master's voice awakens an echo in the disciples which rebounds to enrich the teacher; and thus the Shema recited to oneself generates the returning echo of Prayer.

For in truth, even after the Torah was given, the Blessed Name illuminates at every instant for those who seek Him the individualized path of conduct.

One said: The entire world is sustained by God’s charity, not because it deserves to exist, while the righteous who are far from God’s charity are sustained by force, as due to their own good deeds…’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 10, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 17b) to illuminate his argument here (“as written at the end of the chapter Hayah Koreh (Berakhot 17b). column11: Yevamot 121b: ‘The Sages taught: If one fell into a blazing furnace, one may testify about him that he has died. If he fell into a boiling cauldron filled with wine or oil, one may also testify about him that he has died. In the name of Rabbi Aḥa, they said: If he fell into a cauldron of oil, one may testify about him that he has died, because this ignites the fire even more. Through the force of his fall, oil will splash into the fire and increase the heat of the cauldron. However, if he fell into a cauldron of wine, one may not testify about him that he has died, because when wine splashes into the fire it extinguishes the fire. column11: Berakhot 4a: ‘The Gemara further explores King David’s character. It is said: “A prayer of David…Keep my soul, for I am pious” (Psalms 86:1–2). column11: Avodah Zarah 4b: ‘The Gemara raises a difficulty: If that is so, the prayer of the community should not be recited at that time as well. The Gemara asks: If that is so, then shouldn’t the morning prayer of one who is praying individually also not be recited at this time? The Gemara answers: Since there is in all places a community that prays the morning prayer at that same time, his prayer is not rejected. By contrast, the additional prayer is recited at different times by different communities, as unlike the morning prayer it does not have a fixed time but can be recited at any point during the day.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 10, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Avodah Zarah 4b) to illuminate his argument here (“for he established the yoke of repentance (Avodah Zarah 4b), showing how at times even transgression can be inverted into merits, which is also termed piety that goes beyond the strict letter of the law, representing...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.

column11: Pesachim 119b: ‘Jacob will say to Moses: Take the cup and recite the blessing. Moses will say to them: I will not recite the blessing, as I did not merit to enter Eretz Yisrael, neither in my life nor in my death. Moses will say to Joshua: Take the cup and recite the blessing. Joshua will say to them: I will not recite the blessing, as I did not merit to have a son. column11: Megillah 14b: ‘Nabal, your husband, is a rebel against the throne, as David had already been anointed as king by the prophet Samuel, and Nabal refused his orders. And therefore there is no need to try him, as a rebel is not accorded the ordinary prescriptions governing judicial proceedings. Abigail said to him: You lack the authority to act in this manner, as Saul is still alive. column11: Pesachim 116a: ‘The mishna states that one of the questions is: Why is this night different from all other nights? As on all other nights we dip once; however, on this night we dip twice. column15: That is, one who is foolish, when Hashem gives validation to his service, immediately assumes self-importance and boldness. However, one who is wise claims no personal power for himself, but hedges and disciplines himself all the more.

column11: Pesachim 117a: ‘The Gemara continues to discuss the book of Psalms. If a psalm begins with the terms nitzuaḥ or niggun, this indicates that its praise will be fulfilled in the future. Psalms that begin with the word maskil were delivered by means of a disseminator, a spokesman in a public address. The lecturer would speak softly, followed by a repetition of his discourse in the disseminator’s louder voice, so that everyone could hear. If a psalm begins: Of David a psalm, this teaches that the Divine Presence rested upon him first and afterward he recited the song. However, if a psalm opens with: A psalm of David, this teaches that he first recited the song, and afterward the Divine Presence rested upon him.’ Context and connection to Likkutei Maamarim: In Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Pesachim 117a) to illuminate his argument here (“And the Sages stated in chapter Arvei Pesachim (Pesachim 117a): "A Psalm of David (LeDavid Mizmor)"—first the Shechinah rested upon him, and afterward he uttered song, etc.; for prefixing "Of David" indicates that he...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, Israel's sanctity, and divine service developed in this discourse of Likkutei Maamarim.
